note: Original practice questions for editorial and Android review; not a complete second-midterm course.

questions.stem: What must a launch vehicle provide to place a payload in orbit?
options: Altitude alone, regardless of horizontal speed
Vertical speed alone at any altitude
A suitable altitude with zero horizontal velocity
A suitable position and orbital velocity
questions.explanation: Reaching altitude alone does not establish an orbit: the payload also needs an appropriate velocity.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Kármán line is correct?
options: It marks the altitude at which Earth gravity becomes zero.
It is the altitude of every geostationary satellite.
It separates all atmosphere from a perfect vacuum.
It is a commonly used 100 km boundary, not a sharp end to all atmospheric particles.
questions.explanation: The 100 km line is a convention; the atmosphere becomes progressively thinner and gravity remains present.

questions.stem: What reaction produces the thrust of a rocket in vacuum?
options: The atmosphere pushes the rocket upward.
The rocket accelerates expelled propellant rearward.
The nozzle needs surrounding air to create thrust.
The vehicle gains momentum without expelling mass.
questions.explanation: The vehicle gains momentum in the opposite direction to the exhaust; it does not need air to push against.

questions.stem: For the same initial mass and exhaust velocity, how does using more propellant affect ideal rocket velocity change?
options: It has no effect on the mass ratio.
It decreases the ideal velocity change.
It decreases the exhaust velocity by definition.
It increases the ideal velocity change.
questions.explanation: With initial mass fixed, using more propellant lowers final mass and increases the mass ratio in the ideal rocket equation.

questions.stem: Why can discarding an empty stage help a launch vehicle?
options: It increases the mass remaining to be accelerated.
It makes aerodynamic drag the only remaining force.
The remaining stages no longer accelerate that discarded mass.
It removes the need to carry any propellant.
questions.explanation: Staging reduces the mass carried by later stages, although the discarded structure must first be accelerated.

questions.stem: Which propulsion system usually offers controlled throttling during a burn?
options: A liquid-propellant engine designed for throttling
A conventional solid motor with no throttling mechanism
A spent stage after engine cutoff
Every solid rocket motor
questions.explanation: A suitably designed liquid engine can regulate propellant flow; solid motors typically follow a largely predetermined burn profile.

questions.stem: Why is a near-equatorial site useful for a launch toward the east?
options: All desired orbital inclinations become equally accessible without manoeuvres.
Earth rotation gives the same eastward surface speed at every latitude.
Earth rotation directly cancels the gravitational attraction.
Earth's rotation supplies an initial eastward velocity.
questions.explanation: The launch site already moves eastward with Earth; the achievable benefit depends on location and launch direction.

questions.stem: What does aerodynamic drag do to a vehicle ascending through the atmosphere?
options: It opposes motion relative to the surrounding air.
It always points vertically upward.
It acts in the direction of motion relative to the air.
It vanishes at every altitude below 100 km.
questions.explanation: Aerodynamic drag acts against the vehicle's velocity relative to the local air and contributes to launch losses.

questions.stem: Why can practical launch velocity requirements exceed an ideal orbital-speed estimate?
options: The ideal orbital speed already includes every ascent loss.
Only payload mass, never trajectory, affects ascent requirements.
Atmospheric drag assists ascent throughout the flight.
Gravity and atmospheric drag cause losses during ascent.
questions.explanation: Real ascent is not instantaneous and includes gravity and aerodynamic losses as well as steering effects.

questions.stem: What does the payload fairing mainly protect during atmospheric ascent?
options: The onboard propellant from engine combustion
The empty stage from separation forces
The payload from aerodynamic and thermal loads
The launch site from all rocket exhaust
questions.explanation: A fairing encloses the payload during the dense-atmosphere phase and is normally discarded once it is no longer needed.

questions.stem: Why do astronauts in an orbiting spacecraft experience microgravity?
options: Earth's gravity is exactly zero in low orbit.
Spacecraft and occupants are continually falling around Earth together.
The spacecraft has no mass while orbiting.
The atmosphere pushes them upward.
questions.explanation: The spacecraft and its occupants share approximately the same free-fall trajectory; gravity remains significant in low Earth orbit.

questions.stem: Why are handholds useful inside a spacecraft?
options: They help crew control their position in microgravity.
They increase Earth's gravitational field.
They stop all solar radiation.
They create breathable oxygen.
questions.explanation: Without the usual weight-supported contact with the floor, crew need ways to position and stabilize themselves.

questions.stem: Which risk must a life-support system address in vacuum?
options: The absence of breathable external air
An externally maintained cabin pressure
An unlimited supply of liquid water
Permanent protection from radiation
questions.explanation: A spacecraft or pressure suit must provide a controlled breathable environment and suitable pressure.

questions.stem: What is outgassing?
options: A method of steering with aerodynamic lift
Conversion of sunlight directly into mass
Deliberately increasing the orbital inclination
Release of trapped or volatile substances from a material
questions.explanation: In vacuum, volatile components can leave materials and potentially contaminate sensitive surfaces.

questions.stem: Why can a small debris fragment be dangerous to a spacecraft?
options: Its relative impact speed can be very high.
It always has the mass of a launch vehicle.
It instantly removes Earth's gravity.
It cannot be detected by any means.
questions.explanation: High relative speed can give even a small particle substantial impact energy.

questions.stem: Which combination helps manage collision risk in orbit?
options: Turning off cabin lights only
Pointing the antenna at the ground
Tracking, avoidance manoeuvres and appropriate shielding
Removing all thermal insulation
questions.explanation: Tracking supports avoidance for detectable objects, while shielding helps protect against some smaller impacts.

questions.stem: Why is radiative heat transfer important for an exterior spacecraft surface in vacuum?
options: A spacecraft cannot emit infrared energy.
There is essentially no surrounding gas to provide normal external convection.
Thermal radiation requires dense air.
Every surface in space has the same temperature.
questions.explanation: External convection is negligible in vacuum; surfaces can exchange heat by radiation and conduct heat through structures.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of multilayer insulation on a spacecraft?
options: To stop a rocket's combustion
To create atmospheric lift
To reduce unwanted radiative heat exchange
To generate drinking water directly
questions.explanation: Multilayer insulation limits radiative exchange and is one part of a broader thermal-control design.

questions.stem: Which source can expose a spacecraft to energetic particles?
options: Only reflected sound waves
Solar events and trapped radiation belts
Only the cabin ventilation fan
A shadow that has no particles
questions.explanation: Space radiation can include energetic particles from solar activity, trapped belts and cosmic sources.

questions.stem: Which practice helps reduce the physical effects of long stays in microgravity?
options: A planned exercise programme
Turning off life support
Removing the pressure suit during an EVA
Avoiding all movement
questions.explanation: Regular exercise is one countermeasure used to mitigate changes to muscles and bones during extended spaceflight.

questions.stem: Which spacecraft subsystem supplies electrical power to onboard equipment?
options: The launch fairing
The electrical power subsystem
The thermal protection coating
The orbital debris shield
questions.explanation: The power subsystem generates, stores and distributes electricity.

questions.stem: What does a spacecraft attitude control system regulate?
options: The colour of the launch pad
The chemical composition of Earth’s atmosphere
Its orientation in space
The date of the next solar eclipse
questions.explanation: Attitude is the spacecraft’s orientation; orbit control addresses its trajectory.

questions.stem: What is the role of a spacecraft thermal control system?
options: Make every component exactly 0 °C
Make sunlight the same intensity everywhere
Keep equipment within acceptable temperature limits
Remove the need for electrical power
questions.explanation: Thermal control keeps equipment within the temperature ranges needed for operation.

questions.stem: What is telemetry used for in a space mission?
options: Sending measurements and status information to the ground
Opening the payload fairing before launch
Moving the spacecraft by expelling propellant
Generating oxygen from sunlight
questions.explanation: Telemetry carries measurements and spacecraft status back to mission controllers.

questions.stem: What is an uplink in spacecraft communications?
options: The exhaust from an onboard thruster
A signal sent from the ground to the spacecraft
A signal sent only between two ground antennas
A measurement of solar panel area
questions.explanation: An uplink carries information or commands toward the spacecraft.

questions.stem: How does a flyby differ from an orbiter mission?
options: A flyby must land on the target
A flyby passes the target without entering an orbit around it
A flyby remains fixed above the same surface point indefinitely
An orbiter never observes its target
questions.explanation: A flyby makes observations while passing; an orbiter remains in orbit for repeated observations.

questions.stem: Which vehicle is designed to move across a planetary surface?
options: A flyby probe
A rover
A communications antenna
A launch escape tower
questions.explanation: A rover travels over a surface to make measurements at different locations.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a lander?
options: Replace all ground communication equipment
Measure only the Sun from Earth
Remain permanently in Earth orbit
Reach the surface and operate there
questions.explanation: A lander is designed to reach a surface and perform its mission there.

questions.stem: Why can an atmospheric entry probe need a heat shield?
options: To increase the strength of its radio signal
To produce thrust in a vacuum
To make gravity disappear
To protect it from intense heating during entry
questions.explanation: During fast atmospheric entry, intense heating can damage the vehicle without suitable protection.

questions.stem: What can a balloon drifting in a planetary atmosphere help study?
options: The mechanical strength of a launch tower
The exhaust of every rocket on Earth
The inside of a solid planetary core directly
Atmospheric conditions and circulation
questions.explanation: A drifting balloon can carry sensors and track conditions along its atmospheric path.

questions.stem: What does VTOL describe?
options: An aircraft able to take off and land vertically
An aircraft designed only for short runways
An aircraft designed for sustained supersonic cruise
An aircraft designed to operate only from water
questions.explanation: VTOL means vertical take-off and landing.

questions.stem: What is the main runway advantage of STOL aircraft?
options: They require less distance only after touchdown, not for take-off
They must use a vertical take-off in every operation
They need a longer runway than a comparable conventional aircraft
They can operate using shorter take-off and landing distances
questions.explanation: Short take-off and landing reduces the distance needed compared with conventional operations.

questions.stem: What produces much of a tiltrotor aircraft’s lift during hover?
options: A fixed wing at essentially zero forward airspeed
Buoyancy from a lighter-than-air envelope
Powered rotors directed to produce upward thrust
Lift created mainly by the horizontal tail
questions.explanation: The powered rotors direct thrust upward in hovering flight.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an autogyro rotor in normal forward flight?
options: The rotor is continuously driven by the engine for all lift
The airflow turns the rotor without the rotor being powered for propulsion
The rotor remains locked throughout forward flight
The rotor autorotates only during an engine failure
questions.explanation: An autogyro rotor normally autorotates; a separate propulsion system supplies forward thrust.

questions.stem: What happens to an aircraft flying close to a surface in ground effect?
options: Its induced drag can be lower for a given lift
Its induced drag always increases for a given lift
Its weight decreases as it approaches the ground
Its wing can no longer stall
questions.explanation: The nearby surface modifies the wing flow and can reduce induced drag.

questions.stem: What supports an air-cushion vehicle above the underlying surface?
options: A partial vacuum below the vehicle
Lift generated only by submerged foils
Wheel reactions throughout the cruise
A region of pressurized air
questions.explanation: An air cushion raises pressure below the vehicle and supports its weight.

questions.stem: What supports a hydrofoil craft above the water as it gains speed?
options: Lift generated mainly by the hull sides above water
A pressure cushion created by an air fan
Hydrodynamic lift generated by submerged foils
Buoyancy alone after the hull rises clear of the water
questions.explanation: Submerged foils generate lift in water and raise the hull.

questions.stem: What changes in a tiltwing aircraft when it transitions between hover and forward flight?
options: Only the rotor blades change their chord length
The wing and its propulsors rotate relative to the fuselage
Only the fuselage rotates while the wing stays fixed
The wing remains fixed and only the landing gear tilts
questions.explanation: Tilting the wing changes the direction of its propulsors and wing relative to the fuselage.

questions.stem: Why can vertical take-off be useful for a rescue mission?
options: It permits operation in suitable confined areas without a long runway
It removes the need to check obstacles and landing-area suitability
It guarantees a safe landing in any wind condition
It requires a longer prepared runway than fixed-wing operation
questions.explanation: Vertical operation can reduce dependence on runway length, subject to aircraft and site limits.

questions.stem: What is a practical trade-off in aircraft design?
options: Payload can increase without affecting any other design constraint
Range is independent of fuel and mass
Every mission requires the same optimum configuration
Improving one capability can limit another, such as payload or range
questions.explanation: Payload, range, efficiency and operating constraints influence one another.

questions.stem: What does the collective control primarily change?
options: The pitch of one blade without affecting the others
The cyclic pitch variation around the rotor disk
The pitch of the rotor blades together
The tail-rotor pitch only
questions.explanation: Collective input changes blade pitch together and alters rotor thrust.

questions.stem: What does cyclic control primarily change?
options: The same fixed pitch change on all blades at all azimuths
Rotor blade pitch as a function of blade position around the rotor
The engine fuel flow without changing blade pitch
The physical number of blades during flight
questions.explanation: Cyclic input changes blade pitch around the rotation to tilt the rotor thrust.

questions.stem: Why does a single-main-rotor helicopter need an anti-torque system?
options: The powered main rotor tends to rotate the fuselage in the opposite direction
The main rotor generates only forward thrust
The tail naturally balances all torque without a side force
The reaction torque acts in the same direction as rotor rotation
questions.explanation: An anti-torque system counters the reaction torque and helps control yaw.

questions.stem: Which system commonly provides anti-torque and yaw control?
options: The collective lever acting on the main rotor
The horizontal stabilizer in steady hover
The pitot-static system
A tail rotor
questions.explanation: A tail rotor can provide the side force needed to oppose main-rotor torque and control yaw.

questions.stem: What can keep a helicopter rotor turning during autorotation?
options: The stored fuel pressure alone
Continuous engine torque is always required
Airflow through the rotor during descent
Only the airflow over the horizontal tail
questions.explanation: During autorotation, airflow through the rotor supplies energy to keep it rotating.

questions.stem: What causes a difference in relative airspeed between advancing and retreating blades in forward flight?
options: Only the angle of attack changes; relative speed remains identical
The rotor’s rotation combines with the aircraft’s forward velocity
Blade rotation opposes forward speed on both sides
Only atmospheric density changes between the two sides
questions.explanation: Forward velocity adds to rotational velocity on the advancing side and subtracts on the retreating side.

questions.stem: What can occur if a retreating blade must operate at too high an angle of attack?
options: The blade can stall
Its lift increases indefinitely as angle of attack rises
It cannot produce any aerodynamic drag
The advancing blade must always stall at the same instant
questions.explanation: A blade can stall when its angle of attack exceeds its usable limit.

questions.stem: What is rotor disk loading?
options: Rotor-swept area divided by aircraft weight
Aircraft weight divided by blade chord alone
Engine power divided by the rotor radius
Aircraft weight divided by the area swept by the rotor
questions.explanation: Disk loading relates supported weight to the rotor-swept area.

questions.stem: Why is rotor-tip speed limited?
options: Blade-tip Mach number has no effect on rotor aerodynamics
Increasing tip speed always improves efficiency without limit
High local Mach number can produce compressibility effects
Only the rotational speed of the tail rotor matters
questions.explanation: Increasing tip speed raises local Mach number and can introduce compressibility problems.

questions.stem: What force must approximately balance weight in a steady hover?
options: The upward component of drag alone
The upward component of rotor thrust
The horizontal component of rotor thrust alone
A net upward force much greater than weight throughout steady hover
questions.explanation: In a steady hover, forces approximately balance, including upward thrust and weight.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a guided missile from an unguided rocket?
options: It must have a human pilot
A guidance system can adjust its flight path
It cannot travel through the atmosphere
It never uses a rocket motor
questions.explanation: A guided vehicle can adjust its flight path using a guidance and control system.

questions.stem: What does a propulsion system produce to accelerate a vehicle?
options: Cabin pressure
Wing span
Thrust
Orbital inclination
questions.explanation: Propulsion produces thrust; the vehicle accelerates according to the net force acting on it.

questions.stem: What happens to vehicle mass as onboard propellant is consumed?
options: It always increases
It becomes independent of the remaining propellant
It decreases
It stays exactly constant
questions.explanation: Consumed propellant leaves the vehicle, so the remaining vehicle mass decreases.

questions.stem: What is the role of guidance in a flight vehicle?
options: Replace all of the vehicle structure
Measure the material density of a wing
Generate electricity for cabin lighting
Determine how the desired path should change
questions.explanation: Guidance uses information about the motion and a desired path to determine commands.

questions.stem: What is the role of the flight control system?
options: Provide the entire payload mass
Define sea-level pressure
Make gravity disappear
Carry out commands by adjusting vehicle motion
questions.explanation: The control system acts on the vehicle to change its motion in response to commands.

questions.stem: What force can an aerodynamic control surface produce in air?
options: An aerodynamic force
A permanent change in Earth mass
A force without interacting with air
A change in gravity
questions.explanation: A control surface interacts with the airflow and produces an aerodynamic force and moment.

questions.stem: During an unpowered ballistic coast, which force still acts on the vehicle?
options: A constant force from the battery
Gravity
Thrust from an operating engine
A mandatory force from the launch pad
questions.explanation: Gravity continues to act after engine cutoff; aerodynamic force may also act in an atmosphere.

questions.stem: What does a sensor provide to a guidance system?
options: An automatic removal of aerodynamic drag
A guarantee of perfect knowledge
A replacement for the vehicle mass
Measurements with possible uncertainty
questions.explanation: Sensors provide measurements, which can contain noise or other uncertainty.

questions.stem: Which atmospheric property directly affects dynamic pressure at a given speed?
options: Air density
Dynamic viscosity
Air temperature alone
Speed of sound
questions.explanation: At a given speed, dynamic pressure directly depends on local density; temperature alone does not determine it.

questions.stem: Why can a vehicle use more than one propulsion stage?
options: To avoid any need for energy
To keep total mass constant after burning propellant
To make gravity vanish
To discard mass that is no longer needed
questions.explanation: Staging can discard hardware no longer needed, reducing the mass carried by later stages.
